questions.stem: The part of a flower that produces pollen grains is the
questions.explanation: The anther sits at the top of the stamen and contains pollen sacs in which meiosis produces the pollen grains carrying the male gametes. The filament simply holds it in a position where the pollen can be collected by wind or insects.

distractorRationale.a: The stigma receives pollen; it does not make it
distractorRationale.c: The ovary contains ovules with the female gametes
distractorRationale.d: Sepals protect the flower bud

questions.stem: Which combination of features indicates that a flower is wind pollinated?

options.text: Large coloured petals, sweet scent and abundant nectar
Small dull petals, feathery stigma and large quantities of light dry pollen
Sticky spiky pollen and a small stigma enclosed within the petals
Brightly coloured sepals and anthers hidden deep inside the flower

questions.explanation: Wind cannot be attracted, so colour, scent and nectar would be a waste of resources. Instead the flower exposes hanging anthers to shed light dry pollen and presents a large feathery stigma with a big surface area to intercept grains carried past on the breeze.

distractorRationale.a: Colour, scent and nectar are all devices for attracting animal pollinators
distractorRationale.c: Sticky spiky pollen sticks to insect bodies and would not travel on the wind
distractorRationale.d: Hidden anthers cannot be reached by moving air

questions.stem: After fertilisation in a flowering plant, the ovule develops into the
questions.explanation: Each ovule contains the fertilised egg cell, so each becomes a seed, its outer wall hardening into the testa. The ovary that housed the ovules becomes the fruit, which means a fruit containing five seeds developed from an ovary with five ovules.

distractorRationale.a: The fruit develops from the ovary, not from the ovule
distractorRationale.c: The rest of the flower withers away after fertilisation
distractorRationale.d: The pollen tube is the temporary structure that delivered the male gametes

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes pollination from fertilisation?

options.text: Pollination is the fusion of gametes; fertilisation is the transfer of pollen
Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma; fertilisation is the fusion of the male and female gamete nuclei
Both terms mean the same thing
Pollination occurs only in wind-pollinated plants; fertilisation only in insect-pollinated plants

questions.explanation: Pollination merely delivers pollen to the stigma and may fail to go further — the pollen might be from the wrong species or the plant might be self-sterile. Fertilisation is the later event in which the gamete nuclei actually fuse inside the ovule.

distractorRationale.a: The two definitions have been swapped
distractorRationale.c: They are distinct stages separated by the growth of the pollen tube
distractorRationale.d: Both processes occur in all flowering plants regardless of the pollinating agent

questions.stem: After landing on a compatible stigma, the pollen grain germinates and the pollen tube grows

options.text: down the style to the ovule, where it releases the male gametes
into the nectary to collect sugar

questions.explanation: The pollen tube digests a path down through the style, guided by chemicals from the ovule, and enters the ovule through the micropyle. Its tip then bursts and releases two male gametes, one of which fertilises the egg cell.

distractorRationale.a: The tube grows towards the ovule, which lies below the stigma
distractorRationale.c: Petals play no part in fertilisation and wither after it
distractorRationale.d: The tube obtains nutrients from the style tissue, not from the nectary

questions.stem: A coconut fruit has a thick fibrous husk enclosing an air space. This structure adapts it for dispersal by
questions.explanation: The fibrous husk traps air, so the fruit floats, and it is also waterproof, protecting the seed from salt water. Coconuts can therefore drift along the coast for long distances and still germinate when they are washed ashore.

distractorRationale.a: A coconut is far too heavy to be carried by wind
distractorRationale.c: The husk is not edible and no animal swallows a whole coconut
distractorRationale.d: The fruit does not split violently; it simply falls and floats

questions.stem: Why is the dispersal of seeds away from the parent plant biologically important?

options.text: It prevents the seeds from germinating too early
It reduces competition with the parent for light, water and mineral salts, and lets the species colonise new areas
It increases the number of seeds a plant produces
It guarantees that every seed germinates

questions.explanation: Seedlings crowded under the parent would be shaded and would compete with it and with each other for the same water and minerals, so few would survive. Dispersal spreads the offspring into unoccupied ground and gives the species a chance to spread its range.

distractorRationale.a: Dormancy, not dispersal, controls the timing of germination
distractorRationale.c: Seed number is determined at flowering, before dispersal occurs
distractorRationale.d: Most dispersed seeds still fail; dispersal improves the odds rather than guaranteeing success

questions.stem: A pawpaw plant that bears only male flowers cannot be self-pollinated.
questions.explanation: True. Pawpaw is dioecious, meaning male and female flowers occur on separate plants. A plant bearing only male flowers has no stigma of its own to receive pollen, so its pollen must reach a female plant, which guarantees cross-pollination.

questions.stem: A tomato fruit contains many seeds. What does this tell you about the ovary of the flower from which it developed?

options.text: The ovary contained many ovules, each of which was fertilised
The ovary contained one ovule that divided many times
The flower had many ovaries that fused
Many pollen grains landed on the stigma but none was needed

questions.explanation: Each seed develops from one ovule, so the number of seeds shows the minimum number of ovules that were successfully fertilised. Each of those fertilisations required a separate pollen grain and a separate pollen tube.

distractorRationale.b: An ovule becomes a single seed; it does not divide into several
distractorRationale.c: The tomato flower has one ovary with many ovules in it
distractorRationale.d: Pollen is essential — no fertilisation means no seed

questions.stem: Name the four main parts of a flower and state one function of each. Then give four differences between an insect-pollinated and a wind-pollinated flower, explaining each difference in terms of the pollinating agent.
markingGuide: Calyx of sepals — protects the flower in bud (1 mark); corolla of petals — attracts pollinators by colour and scent (1 mark); androecium of stamens — anthers produce pollen containing the male gametes (1 mark); gynoecium of carpels — the ovary contains ovules with the female gametes and the stigma receives pollen (1 mark)
Difference 1: petals large and coloured versus small, green or absent, because insects must be attracted visually while wind cannot be (2 marks)
Difference 2: scent and nectar present versus absent, because these are rewards and signals for animal visitors only (2 marks)

Difference 3: pollen small in quantity, large, sticky or spiky versus abundant, small, light, smooth and dry, because insect transfer is targeted while wind transfer is wasteful and needs buoyant grains (2 marks)

Difference 4: anthers and stigma enclosed within the flower versus long, exposed and hanging outside with a feathery stigma, because insects enter the flower while wind must reach the anthers and be intercepted by a large stigma (2 marks)
questions.explanation: Each difference should be justified by the requirements of the pollinating agent rather than simply listed, since the marks are for the reasoning. The core principle is that attraction features exist only where a living pollinator must be persuaded to visit, while wind-pollinated flowers invest instead in exposure and in sheer quantity of light pollen.

questions.stem: Which part of the flower is responsible for attracting pollinators?
questions.explanation: The petals of a flower are typically brightly colored and fragrant, which helps attract pollinators such as bees and butterflies. This attraction is crucial for the process of pollination, which leads to fertilization and the production of seeds.

distractorRationale.b: The stamen is the male reproductive part, primarily involved in producing pollen, not attracting pollinators.
distractorRationale.c: Sepals protect the flower bud before it opens but do not play a role in attracting pollinators.
distractorRationale.d: The ovary is involved in seed development after fertilization, not in attracting pollinators.

questions.stem: What is the primary role of the stigma in the reproductive process of flowering plants?
questions.explanation: The stigma is the part of the flower that receives pollen during the process of pollination. It is typically sticky to facilitate the adherence of pollen grains, allowing for successful fertilization.

distractorRationale.a: Pollen is produced by the anthers, not the stigma.
distractorRationale.c: The ovule is protected by the ovary, not the stigma.
distractorRationale.d: The formation of fruit occurs after fertilization, involving the ovary, not the stigma.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of insect-pollinated flowers?
questions.explanation: Insect-pollinated flowers often have a strong fragrance to attract pollinators. These flowers are typically brightly colored and have a structure that makes it easy for insects to access the nectar and pollen.

distractorRationale.a: Small, dull-colored petals are typical of wind-pollinated flowers, which do not rely on visual attraction.
distractorRationale.c: While insect-pollinated flowers do produce pollen, they do not need to produce as much as wind-pollinated flowers.
distractorRationale.d: Long, feathery stigmas are characteristic of wind-pollinated flowers to catch airborne pollen.

questions.stem: During fertilization in flowering plants, what does the pollen tube carry?
questions.explanation: The pollen tube carries sperm cells from the pollen grain to the ovule inside the ovary. This process is essential for fertilization, where one sperm cell fuses with the ovule to form a zygote.

distractorRationale.a: Nutrients are not carried by the pollen tube; they are provided by the plant.
distractorRationale.c: Ovules are the structures that develop into seeds after fertilization, not carried by the pollen tube.
distractorRationale.d: Pollen grains are the source of sperm cells, not what the pollen tube carries.

questions.stem: What is the role of fruit in flowering plants?
questions.explanation: The primary role of fruit in flowering plants is to protect the developing seeds and aid in their dispersal. Fruits can take various forms and may attract animals that help in spreading the seeds away from the parent plant.

distractorRationale.a: Photosynthesis is carried out by leaves, not fruit.
distractorRationale.b: Attracting pollinators is primarily the role of flowers, not fruits.
distractorRationale.d: Nectar is produced by flowers to attract pollinators, not by fruits.

provenance.note: Exam-pattern questions generated with OpenAI against the NERDC/WAEC/NECO/JAMB syllabus.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a method of seed dispersal?
questions.explanation: Self-pollination refers to the process where a flower's pollen fertilizes its own ovules, not a method of seed dispersal. In contrast, wind, water, and animals are all methods by which seeds can be dispersed away from the parent plant.

distractorRationale.a: Wind dispersal is a common method where seeds are carried away by the wind.
distractorRationale.b: Water dispersal involves seeds being carried by water bodies.
distractorRationale.d: Animal dispersal occurs when animals eat fruits and excrete the seeds elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of wind-pollinated flowers?
questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers often have feathery stigmas that can capture pollen carried by the wind. These flowers typically lack bright colors and fragrances since they do not rely on pollinators for reproduction.

distractorRationale.a: Brightly colored petals are characteristic of insect-pollinated flowers.
distractorRationale.b: Sticky pollen is more common in insect-pollinated flowers to adhere to pollinators.
distractorRationale.d: Strong fragrance is also associated with insect-pollinated flowers to attract them.

questions.stem: What happens to the ovary after fertilization in flowering plants?
questions.explanation: After fertilization, the ovary of a flowering plant develops into a fruit, which contains the seeds. This transformation is essential for protecting the seeds and aiding in their dispersal.

distractorRationale.a: The ovary does not wither away; it undergoes transformation into fruit.
distractorRationale.c: Seeds develop from ovules, not from the ovary itself.
distractorRationale.d: The ovary does not produce more ovules after fertilization.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about seed dispersal is true?

options.text: Seeds are always dispersed by wind.
Seed dispersal helps reduce competition among plants.
All seeds are dispersed immediately after they are formed.
Seed dispersal has no effect on plant distribution.

questions.explanation: Seed dispersal is crucial as it helps reduce competition among plants by spreading them over a wider area. This increases the chances of survival for the seeds as they grow in different locations.

distractorRationale.a: Seeds can be dispersed by various methods including wind, water, and animals.
distractorRationale.c: Not all seeds are dispersed immediately; some may remain in the parent plant until conditions are favorable.
distractorRationale.d: Seed dispersal significantly affects plant distribution and biodiversity.

questions.stem: In flowering plants, what is the role of the anther?
questions.explanation: The anther is the part of the stamen that produces pollen grains, which contain the male gametes necessary for fertilization. The release of pollen is a critical step in the reproduction of flowering plants.

distractorRationale.a: Ovules are produced in the ovary, not the anther.
distractorRationale.b: Nectar is produced by specialized glands, not by the anther.
distractorRationale.d: While the anther contributes to reproduction, its primary function is not to attract pollinators.

questions.stem: Which of the following processes occurs first during the reproduction of flowering plants?
questions.explanation: Pollination occurs first in the reproductive process of flowering plants, where pollen is transferred from the anther to the stigma. This is followed by fertilization, fruit formation, and ultimately seed dispersal.

distractorRationale.a: Fertilization occurs after pollination when the pollen tube reaches the ovule.
distractorRationale.c: Seed dispersal happens last, after seeds have developed in the fruit.
distractorRationale.d: Fruit formation occurs after fertilization, not before.

questions.stem: Which part of the flower is primarily responsible for producing ovules?
questions.explanation: The ovary is the part of the flower that contains the ovules, which develop into seeds after fertilization. It plays a crucial role in the reproductive process of flowering plants.

distractorRationale.a: The stigma is responsible for receiving pollen but does not produce ovules.
distractorRationale.b: The style connects the stigma to the ovary but does not produce ovules.
distractorRationale.d: The filament supports the anther and does not have a role in ovule production.

questions.stem: In flowering plants, what is the significance of cross-pollination compared to self-pollination?

options.text: It occurs only in wind-pollinated flowers.
It is less efficient than self-pollination.

questions.explanation: Cross-pollination involves the transfer of pollen from one flower to another, leading to greater genetic variation in the offspring. This diversity can enhance adaptability and resilience in changing environments.

distractorRationale.a: Cross-pollination typically results in more seeds due to increased fertilization chances.
distractorRationale.c: Cross-pollination can occur in both insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers.
distractorRationale.d: Although self-pollination can be efficient, cross-pollination generally leads to better genetic outcomes.

questions.stem: What is the primary function of the petals in a flower?
questions.explanation: Petals are often brightly colored and serve to attract pollinators, which is essential for the process of pollination. Their visual appeal can guide insects and other pollinators to the flower.

distractorRationale.a: While some flowers do produce nectar, the primary role of petals is attraction.
distractorRationale.c: The ovary is typically protected by the sepals, not the petals.
distractorRationale.d: The structure of the flower is supported by the peduncle and receptacle.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describes fertilization in flowering plants?

options.text: It occurs when pollen lands on the stigma.
It involves the fusion of male and female gametes.
It is the process of seed dispersal.
It leads directly to the formation of fruit.

questions.explanation: Fertilization in flowering plants is defined as the fusion of male gametes from the pollen with female gametes in the ovule, resulting in the formation of a zygote. This is a crucial step in the reproductive cycle before fruit formation.

distractorRationale.a: Pollen landing on the stigma is part of pollination, not fertilization.
distractorRationale.c: Seed dispersal occurs after fertilization and fruit formation.
distractorRationale.d: Fruit formation occurs after fertilization, not directly as a result of it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of insect-pollinated flowers?
questions.explanation: Insect-pollinated flowers typically produce moderate amounts of pollen since they rely on insects for transfer rather than wind. Large quantities of pollen are more characteristic of wind-pollinated flowers, which must produce enough to ensure some reaches a stigma.

distractorRationale.a: Bright colors attract insects to the flower.
distractorRationale.b: Fragrance is a common trait to lure pollinators.
distractorRationale.d: Nectar serves as a reward for insects visiting the flower.

questions.stem: What is the role of the sepal in a flower?
questions.explanation: Sepals are the outer parts of the flower that protect the developing bud before it opens. They serve as a protective layer for the delicate flower parts inside.

distractorRationale.a: Pollen is produced by the anther, not the sepal.
distractorRationale.b: Attraction of pollinators is primarily the role of petals.
distractorRationale.d: Fertilization involves the ovary and pollen, not the sepal.

questions.stem: Which agent of seed dispersal is characterized by the use of wind?
questions.explanation: Winged seeds are adapted for dispersal by wind as their shape allows them to be carried over long distances. This adaptation increases the chances of successful germination in suitable environments.

distractorRationale.b: Water dispersal typically involves buoyant seeds, not wind.
distractorRationale.c: Explosive mechanisms involve the rapid release of seeds, not wind.

questions.stem: Which of the following processes occurs after fertilization in flowering plants?
questions.explanation: After fertilization, the ovary develops into a fruit, which contains the seeds. This process is essential for protecting the seeds and aiding in their eventual dispersal.

distractorRationale.a: Pollination occurs before fertilization.
distractorRationale.b: Seed dispersal happens after fruit formation.
distractorRationale.d: Germination is the process that occurs after seeds are dispersed.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of fruit in flowering plants?

options.text: To provide nourishment to the flower
To protect seeds and aid in dispersal

questions.explanation: The primary purpose of fruit is to protect the seeds and facilitate their dispersal. Fruits can attract animals that help in the dispersal process by consuming the fruit and excreting the seeds elsewhere.

distractorRationale.a: Attraction of pollinators is the role of flowers, not fruits.
distractorRationale.b: Nourishment is provided during the flowering stage, not by the fruit.
distractorRationale.d: Pollen production is the function of the anther, not the fruit.

questions.explanation: The nectary is the specialized gland in flowers that produces nectar, which attracts pollinators such as bees and butterflies. This mutualistic relationship enhances the chances of successful pollination.

distractorRationale.a: The anther produces pollen, not nectar.
distractorRationale.b: The stigma receives pollen but does not produce nectar.

questions.explanation: Floating seeds are adapted for dispersal by water, allowing them to travel to new locations. This method is particularly effective in aquatic environments where seeds can float on water bodies.
